item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Downvoted, a lot of issues here.

1- This is Safe. Put it in a box, it does nothing and is contained forever.

2- First paragraph of Containment is just garbage. Too many words to say "under Standard Procedure", and though it hints to a past of distinct procedures, this past is never relevant or cited.

3- Second paragraph of Containment is too cumbersome. It could be a lot cleaner and still say that the Procedures are more to give access than to keep the thing locked.

4- First paragraph of Description is hugely thorough on describing how it was dirty, but the Foundation cleaned it. We hardly have to know this, and it could even be said with far less words.

5- The description of the Genovese case could be cleaned, corrected (she lived with a partner), and the Expungements changed to black-boxes for ease of reading. By the way, it would be better for it to be the point where the Foundation noticed and apprehended the object, instead of sounding like just some historical trivia thrown in the article.

6- The tone is excessively informal on the following paragraphs, and the entire Recovery Incident not only needs less amazement and more professionalism from the Foundation, it should be included in the main article.

7- The last two paragraphs of Description should be completely replaced by a clearer description of standard recovery protocol, or better yet, such description could be moved to Containment section.

8- Addendum A could far more clinical or be removed if the previous suggestion is taken.

9- Every other addenda could be replaced by a Tale about the Omega Project, but have no reason whatsoever to be here.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I've always had kind of mixed feelings towards this one? The concept is definitely interesting, and I like the idea that an event could actually create an scp rather than be caused by it, but the fact that a lot of this article's content/effect hinges on the Genovese murder is kind of tacky (and maybe slightly tasteless, considering that a large factor in the witness' non-reactions may have been that the victim was outwardly gay in a time when that wasn't considered acceptable.)
There are also some sections that could definitely use some tweaking in regards to tone ("What is clear, however" just seems too informal a transition to me?)
Also it's a small thing, but the fact that the foundation cleaned the knife for "aesthetic purposes" seems… wrong, I guess? It just doesn't strike me as something the foundation would do. I don't think they'd be hugely concerned with keeping artifacts pretty.
Finally, if we're going by the lock-box test, shouldn't this be a safe item? It is admittedly dangerous when wielded, but it has no autonomy, and when locked away has no power to do, well, anything.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The object itself is interesting, but as others have stated, there are issues with some of the writing and major issues with the object's background.

I think the article would probably be a lot better if one were to cut out all information on the knife's background, remove the Omega-7 addenda, and then very briefly summarize the object's discovery and retrieval. As it stands, the effect, its containment, and the retrieval are all very clever and set up some super interesting "rules" for the object; but I feel the reliance on an urban legend, the warnings against obviously bad cross-tests, and the pointlessly edgy gore (redactions notwithstanding) in the incident report all take away from the article.

They aren't just bad in and of themselves; they also pad the length out considerably and are a distraction from the real "meat" of the article. Short and sweet would work much better.

Downvoted.

First of all, it makes no sense for Kitty Genovese's name to be expunged. It's not hidden knowledge. This case is widespread public knowledge. It's one of the most famous examples - if not the most famous example - of the bystander effect. It was even referenced in Watchmen.

But as stated, it's an SCP that's not scary because the bystander effect is far scarier. This idea shortchanges a very chilling fact about human psychology.

The first recorded appearance of SCP-668 was in the 1960s, during the infamous [DATA EXPUNGED] case. [DATA EXPUNGED], a New York woman living alone, was allegedly raped and murdered by subject [DATA EXPUNGED].

No.

Attributing an SCP to a real life event like this both cheapens it and the article. It's crude, dismissive of the victims, and a cheap dodge of humanity's very real capacity to do horrible things to each other.

item.title: Re: Fussiness
item.content:encoded:
I know I'm necro'ing this but the psych major in me wants to expand on that nitpicking — most of those 38 witnesses knew nothing more than that they'd heard screaming, it's the middle of the night, you hear some screams, can't make them out, you gonna go call the cops or roll over and try to go back to bed?

On the other hand, you have the doorman who basically watched the whole damned thing and then took a nap, and the guy whose stairway she ended up in. The former? OD end swearing to excess if I went there, the latter? Was drunk, and was the one to eventually get the cops to her.

That aside, I really like the implications those little tidbit provide. You could watch a murder, think nothing of it, and then have to live the rest of your life knowing that you could've stopped it. This thing could ruin the lives of scores of people with one murder, if it happened in a public enough location. For me, that's what makes this truly terrifying — watching someone I love be murdered would be bad enough, but to not try to do anything and then have to live with that? Nightmare fuel.

item.title: Fussiness
item.content:encoded:
First, there's the general dislike for directly blaming an SCP for a specific historical tragedy — although I'll grant that "whether the item received its properties due to this event, or whether it had them beforehand, is a matter of debate" is a decent attempt to cover your authorial ass in this respect.

Second, there's the general disapproval of expungement in containment procedures; I'll grant that it's a relic of the earlier days of the site, when we were looser with terminology and strict logic.

Third, there's the fact that the Genovese murder (and don't give me any Montaukish bullshit about how this isn't necessarily the Genovese murder; there's enough detail supplied to make it indisputable) didn't actually happen that way. It wasn't 38 people watching and not doing anything. People did call the police as it was happening; it was a huge clusterfuck, some people came outside and scared Moseley away, the police were called, she staggered to a new location , people lost track of her (because it was nearly 3 AM and not all the streetlights were working), Moseley came back and attacked her a second time, and eventually she died in the arms of some neighbors who came out to help.

There was at least one neighbor who admitted to having told her husband "don't call the police, there must have been twenty other people who called the police". But many other people did call the police as it was happening. They just didn't get there in time.

item.title: Object Class
item.content:encoded:
I really liked the concept and the simple, yet horrifying nature of 668. The text is well-written and having narratives of incidents where the item was involved amongst civilians really added to the immersion.

I have one objection though. This shouldn't be classified as Euclid, even though it's an extremely dangerous item, it only is so at the hands of a human or humanoid being bearing violent will towards others. Also, considering how well know are its properties (except for range of effect), it fails the locked box test. That being said, SCP-668 should be classified as Safe (as long as access is strictly controlled).

item.title: Infinite range
item.content:encoded:
Maybe it's my professional bias but come on, man… Scientific improbability of a force having infinite effective range aside, this would imply the knife being able to, for example, prevent aliens from a far-away planet from destroying Earth. However cool that may be (who knows, maybe this SCP is the only reason why we are still around!), this would be way over the top.

Then again, what the hell. Upvoted. I have suspended my disbelief for worse, the issue of range has provided some good narrativium and the whole thing is excellent.

One question: is "the only non Omega-7 recovery" case mentioned in the main text related to the separately-reported incident? Because as far as I can tell, the descriptions are inconsistent if so and the former is not the only such incident if not.
